title: OS Credential Dumping: Cached Domain Credentials
shortTitle: OS Credential Dumping: Cached Domain Credentials
summary: Cached Domain Credentials are hashes Windows keeps locally so a user can still sign in when no domain controller is reachable. On current Windows versions the format is the domain cached credentials version two hash, sometimes called MS-Cache, and it cannot be replayed directly in a pass the hash style attack, so the adversary has to crack it offline to recover the plaintext. System rights are needed to read the cache, normally by saving the SECURITY hive or reading it from memory while the system runs. On Linux, directory integration software keeps equivalent caches in local database files that serve the same purpose. Detection looks at hive exports, reads of the cache database, and later successful authentication with a recovered password. The number of cached logons is a configuration choice, so limiting it reduces exposure.

beginner.definition: Windows can remember domain logins so you can still sign in when the network is down. Those remembered details are called cached credentials. This sub-technique means stealing that cache. It differs from the parent because the stolen data cannot be used directly and must be cracked first.
beginner.whyItMatters: Offline sign in is convenient, but it leaves a local copy of your login data. If an attacker steals that copy, they may recover real passwords over time. Because the data cannot be reused directly, cracking can take a while. Weak passwords fall quickly, so the risk is real for many users. Limiting how many logins are cached reduces this exposure.
howItWorks: A user signs in to a domain, and Windows keeps a local copy of the login data.
That copy allows sign in later even when no domain controller can be reached.
An attacker with system rights saves the hive that holds this cache.
The saved data is taken elsewhere and processed with password cracking tools.
Cracking guesses passwords repeatedly until one matches the stored hash.
The attacker then signs in as that user using the recovered password.
beginner.example: Imagine a shared flat where the front door needs a code, but the building network is often down. Each flatmate writes their own code on a note kept in a locked drawer. A visitor who opens the drawer copies the notes. The codes are written in a form they cannot use directly. They must work out each real code by trial and error. Cached credentials are those written notes.
takeaways: Cached credentials are hashes that need cracking, not direct reuse.
Fewer cached logons on a device means less material available to steal.
Watch hive exports and later logins made with recovered passwords.

objectives: Explain why Windows caches domain credentials on a local device.
Describe why cached hashes cannot be replayed and must be cracked instead.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from the credential dumping parent.
Identify artefacts left when the cache is exported or read.
Explain how cached logon settings change the exposure of a device.
